The channel speaks a language-agnostic wire protocol, so the process at the other end does not have to be R.
[pymizu](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/pymizu) is the Python binding of the same shared-memory core, and a channel connects the two languages as directly as two R sessions.
Pass the peer program as a source string (instead of a quoted expression) and set the launcher to `mizu_py_launcher()` — it checks for the interpreter and pymizu before the channel is created, then spawns `python3 -m pymizu.child`.
Here a Python echo loop, mirroring the R one in [Channels](channels.html) (runs when a `python3` with pymizu and NumPy installed is on the `PATH`):

``` r
library(mizu)

ch <- mizu_channel(
  "
import pymizu
while True:
    x = ch.recv(30)
    if pymizu.is_sentinel(x):
        break
    ch.send(x * 2)
",
  launcher = mizu_py_launcher()
)

mizu_send(ch, c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5))
mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5)
#> [1] 3 5 7
mizu_close(ch)
```

The exchange is easiest to take in tiers, from the everyday to the involved: most values cross as an ordinary copy and round-trip unchanged, past a size floor larger data crosses without copying at all, and a handful of types have no faithful home on the other side and stay put.
A closing fine-print section collects the few round-trip normalizations and what your Python collaborator sees.

## Everyday values round-trip

Most R objects cross as an ordinary copy and come back `identical()`.
Python sees the natural equivalent — a NumPy array for a vector, a dict for a named list — and whatever Python sends back arrives as the natural R object:

- Atomic vectors — `logical`, `integer`, `double`, `complex`, `character`, and `raw`, plus `integer64` (bit64’s exact layout, constructed without bit64) — cross both ways: `c(1.5, 2.5)` arrives in Python as a `float64` array and returns as the same `numeric()`.
- Strings cross as strings: `NA_character_` reads as `None` in Python, and Python `None` comes back as `NULL`.
- Lists cross as Python lists, named lists as dicts with string keys, and back.
- A `Date`, `POSIXct`, or `difftime` keeps its meaning — Python works with it as a `datetime64` or `timedelta64` array.
- A matrix or array keeps its dimensions.
- Labels ride along: a named vector keeps its names, and a matrix or array keeps its `dimnames` — axis names included, so a `table` arrives with its class and every axis label intact.
  An unmodified round trip is `identical()`.
  Names ride on the plain atomic types; the exceptions are listed in what doesn’t cross.
- A data frame crosses to a Python frame and back — see the data frame section below.

The few cases where a round trip normalizes the container (never the values) are listed in the fine print.

## Large data crosses without copying

Past a size floor, the data itself never moves: it is written to shared memory once, and both sides read it in place — no copy, no parsing.
Everything you *receive* large arrives as an ALTREP view over the shared pages — exactly the zero-copy mechanism you get from another R process — and everything you *send* large arrives in Python backed by those same pages:

- A large `numeric`, `integer`, `raw`, `complex`, or `integer64` vector.
- A large character vector (sent by Python as a `list[str | None]`, `None` as `NA_character_`).
- A large matrix or array — C order, Fortran order, or strided, the data never transposed — and a large `datetime64` array, which arrives as a `Date` or `POSIXct` view with `NaT` as `NA`.
- A large nested Python tree of lists, dicts, arrays, and strings, arriving as a list view over one shared region.
- A large data frame, crossing as one shared-memory region in both directions — see the data frame and Arrow sections below.

The floors: a flat vector on a channel crosses as a view from 256 KB — below that it takes one quick copy into the channel’s spill arena, cheaper than region machinery at that size.
Everywhere else — pools, string vectors, frames, anything with `dim` — the floor is 32 KB.

Views compose: a received view sent back crosses as its region’s name alone — zero payload bytes — and the receiver resolves a view of the original region.
The same holds for a data frame echoed unmodified, even through polars or pyarrow; modify some columns in between and only those columns cross as data, the rest still by reference.

## What doesn’t cross

A value with no faithful home on the other side is declined at `mizu_send()` with a `mizu_error_not_portable` naming the path and reason.
The channel stays usable.

- `POSIXlt`, a character matrix, and S4 objects stay on R’s side.
- A named vector with a class or of character type — a named character vector, factor, `Date`, or `POSIXct`, standalone or as a frame column — declines: names ride only on the plain atomic vectors.
  A named list of strings crosses fine, as a Python dict.
- A data.table (its internal self-reference pointer is not portable), a groupedData-style frame (a formula attribute is not either), an ordered-factor column, and a column that is itself a labeled matrix.
- From the Python side: Arrow nested, decimal, `date64`, `time`, and `interval` columns, and ordered dictionaries — cast a polars `Enum` to `pl.Categorical` first.

## The fine print

A round trip can normalize the container, never the values:

- A standalone factor comes back as character strings (inside a data frame it stays a factor, crossing as a dictionary-encoded column).
- A length-1 `NA` — `NA`, `NA_integer_`, `NA_character_` — comes back as `NULL`, matching Python `None`.
- A logical vector with missing values comes back as integer — `c(TRUE, NA)` returns as `c(1L, NA)` — NumPy having no missing-aware bool dtype.
- A `POSIXct` timezone normalizes to `"UTC"` (the instant is exact), and `difftime` units normalize to seconds — a minute crosses as 60 seconds.
- A `uint64` value past 2^53 crosses as `NA` with a warning at send, and `INT32_MIN` or `INT64_MIN` in an integer array reads as `NA` — those bit patterns are R’s own `NA` sentinels.

And for what your Python collaborator sees on their side:

- A vector arrives as a NumPy array — `float64`, `int32`, `uint8`, `complex128`, or `int64` to match.
  NumPy arrays of other numeric dtypes convert at send time and cross as a copy at any size; the [dtype matrix](https://shikokuchuo.net/pymizu/user-guide/interop.html#the-dtype-matrix) on the pymizu site has the exact per-dtype correspondence, widening rows included.
- Labels live on `pymizu.DimArray`, an `ndarray` subclass.
  NumPy operations drop them rather than risk mislabeling reshaped data, so a modified array comes back as a plain array — re-attach labels in Python and they ride back as `names` or `dimnames`.
- A data frame arrives as a `pymizu.Frame` — the next section has the details.

## Data frames

A data frame crosses as a `pymizu.Frame` — a column dict on the Python side, one `pl.from_arrow(f)` or `pa.table(f)` away from polars or pyarrow — and a polars, pyarrow, or pandas frame arrives back as a `data.frame`.
Past the zero-copy floor the frame travels as one shared-memory region in both directions: no copy, no parse, numeric columns read in place.
The full dtype contract, with the NA-sentinel and widening rules per dtype, is the [dtype matrix](https://shikokuchuo.net/pymizu/user-guide/interop.html#the-dtype-matrix) on the pymizu site.

Frame metadata rides along verbatim.
The full class vector (a tibble’s `c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")`, any class ending in `"data.frame"`) and extra attributes such as a `reference` note or readr’s column specification cross opaquely: Python stashes them undecoded on the `pymizu.Frame`, and an unmodified echo restores them, so a pristine round trip is `identical()`.
The stash rides the pristine received frame only: a frame rebuilt through pyarrow, polars, pandas, or `from_arrow` arrives in R as a plain `data.frame`.

## Arrow data

The frame exchange extends to Arrow producers directly: an `arrow` Table, RecordBatch, or RecordBatchReader — and any struct-typed `nanoarrow_array_stream` or `nanoarrow_array`, which covers `DBI::dbGetQueryArrow()`, duckdb, adbc, and polars outputs — stages straight off the Arrow buffers, one layout write into the shared region rather than a conversion to R values first.

The same path serves pools: an Arrow tabular returned from a task crosses as one frame region, and one nested in a payload — a list element, a task argument, the spliced task expression itself — crosses by reference, the received object holding a view in place of the table.

The receiver gets an ordinary `data.frame`, each column a view over the region’s pages, and `mizu_as_arrow()` converts back to Arrow: a struct-typed `nanoarrow_array_stream` whose buffers point straight into the shared region for attribute-free double, integer, `integer64`, and character columns, the rest (factors, Date / POSIXct / difftime, logical, raw) converting per column.

A subset frame, or a new data frame assembled from received columns, keeps the backing pages — the export borrows each column through its original region, and a column re-sent inside a new frame crosses by reference, not by copy.
If a region’s producer exited, only that region’s columns fall back to the copy path.

``` r
ch <- mizu_channel(quote(mizu_send(ch, mizu_recv(ch))))
mizu_send(ch, arrow::arrow_table(data.frame(x = runif(1e5), s = rep(c("a", "b", NA), length.out = 1e5))))

df <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
stream <- mizu_as_arrow(df)
arrow::as_arrow_table(stream)
#> Table
#> 100000 rows x 2 columns
#> $x <double>
#> $s <large_string>

# a subset, or a new frame assembled from received columns, borrows the same pages
sub <- df["x"]
arrow::as_arrow_table(mizu_as_arrow(sub))
#> Table
#> 100000 rows x 1 columns
#> $x <double>
mixed <- data.frame(x = df$x, y = runif(1e5))
arrow::as_arrow_table(mizu_as_arrow(mixed))
#> Table
#> 100000 rows x 2 columns
#> $x <double>
#> $y <double>
mizu_close(ch)
```

The same bytes reach a Python peer as a `pymizu.Frame`, where `pa.table(f)` / `pl.from_arrow(f)` consume them with no export step at all.

Two things to know: sending a stream consumes it — a streaming RecordBatchReader is fully materialized at send, source bytes and region resident at once — and fidelity is frame-level, not Arrow-schema-exact (a dictionary returns as a factor, uints widen, an `int32` of `INT32_MIN` reads as `NA`, and a `uint64` past 2^53 crosses as `NA` with a warning at send — firing on the worker for a pool publish, invisible to the submitter).

A `timestamp[ns]` or `duration[ns]` column arrives as a `POSIXct` or `difftime` in seconds: the nanosecond counts cross verbatim and convert to doubles with `count * 1e-9` — the same conversion the µs-rounded form uses, so the values are identical bit for bit, and only sub-microsecond resolution is lost.

## Mixed-language pools

Channels move values; pools move computation. A pool’s workers can be Python processes too, and you drive them with a language-neutral task description.
`mizu_py_pool_launcher()` spawns the workers (checking for the interpreter like the channel launcher), `mizu_call()` builds the task — a qualified `"mod.fn"` name or a `.source =` string, plus constant arguments — and `mizu_submit_call()` submits it:

``` r
p <- mizu_pool(2L, launcher = mizu_py_pool_launcher())
t <- mizu_submit_call(p, mizu_call("numpy.quantile", runif(100), q = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)))
mizu_collect(t)
#> [1] 0.1872429 0.5569842 0.7464803
s <- mizu_submit_call(p, mizu_call(.source = "y = x * 2\ny + 1", x = 20))
mizu_collect(s)
#> [1] 41
mizu_pool_stop(p)
```

Unnamed arguments map to the positional list and named ones to the named dict, matching Python’s `*args, **kwargs`; a `.source =` task evaluates in a fresh namespace with the named arguments bound as names and the result as the trailing expression’s value.

The pool knows its workers’ language, so there is nothing to set: a plain `mizu_submit()` on a Python pool fails with an error pointing you to `mizu_submit_call()`, an unqualified name fails at submit, and a non-portable argument raises `mizu_error_not_portable` at submit.
Task errors cross as `mizu_error_remote` conditions with the remote type preserved, and a result without a portable home fails the task with one naming the type.

Arguments follow the same rules as channel payloads: a fresh array past the 32 KB floor crosses as one shared-memory view rather than a copy, and an argument that is already a shared view (received from a channel, a pool result, or a `mori::share()`d vector) crosses as its identifier alone — zero payload bytes.
If the workers are too old to read such references, the submit fails with an error naming the remedy.

The reverse direction mirrors: `pymizu.Pool.create()` with `pymizu.r_pool_launcher()`, and `Pool.submit()` with `pymizu.call()` specs.

## The cross-language map

You can also pass a `mizu_call()` spec as `mizu_map()`’s `.f` to map a Python function over an R vector — the cross-language map.
Each element of `.x` becomes the spec’s first positional argument (a `"mod.fn"` spec) or binds as `x` (a `.source =` spec), and constant arguments stay in the spec itself, so `...` stays empty.
`.template`, `.collect = "view"`, and `.seed` work as they do on a same-language map; each worker language derives its own random streams from the seed, so results are reproducible for a given worker language but not identical across languages:

``` r
p <- mizu_pool(2L, launcher = mizu_py_pool_launcher())
mizu_map(p, runif(6), mizu_call("numpy.quantile", q = c(0.25, 0.75)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0.5051453 0.5051453
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 0.2117105 0.2117105
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] 0.3709099 0.3709099
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> [1] 0.8677452 0.8677452
#> 
#> [[5]]
#> [1] 0.6673288 0.6673288
#> 
#> [[6]]
#> [1] 0.5521507 0.5521507
mizu_map(p, runif(6), mizu_call("numpy.log"), .template = numeric(1))
#> [1] -0.2213433 -1.6208470 -0.8452594 -0.8991134 -0.1003950 -0.9736976
mizu_pool_stop(p)
```

A labeled array as the map’s `x` drops its labels, as it would on a same-language map.
